The luminous cardinalfish Rhabdamia gracilis is a small apogonid species found across Indo-Pacific coral reefs. Field surveys indicate that adults attain a maximum standard length of 7.4 cm [Li = 7.4 cm], a modest size consistent with its position as a mid-sized member of the cardinalfish family. This ultimate body dimension appears to be reached within the first year of life under optimal thermal conditions. The age and size at which individuals transition from the juvenile phase into the reproductively active population is marked by a distinct standard length of 3.6 cm [Lp = 3.6 cm] at puberty. This threshold corresponds to a body mass of roughly 0.56 grams [Wwp = roughly 0.56 grams] when estimated from local length-weight regressions. The onset of sexual maturation thus occurs when the fish has achieved approximately half of its maximal somatic dimensions, a pattern that reflects the typical allocation strategy of iteroparous reef fishes.

Reproductive output in this species has been estimated through comparative studies with the closely related congener Apogon imberbis. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C], females of Rhabdamia gracilis produce an annual total of approximately 14 offspring per individual per year [Ri = approximately 14 offspring per individual per year]. This value is derived from an average clutch size of 1 egg per clutch [N_R_i = 1 egg per clutch], with females typically completing about 14 spawning events per year [F_R_i = about 14 spawning events per year]. The modest fecundity per event is characteristic of apogonids, which invest relatively heavily in each offspring through extended oral brooding. The total annual reproductive output, integrated over the breeding season, places this species on the slower end of the life-history continuum among tropical reef fishes.

The early life stages of Rhabdamia gracilis begin with the release of small, pelagic eggs that undergo rapid development. At the moment of hatching, each yolk-sac larva possesses a wet weight at birth of 0.0001438 grams [Wwb = 0.0001438 grams], a figure derived from the average egg diameter of 650 micrometres observed in related species. This minute initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the embryo, necessitating an early transition to exogenous feeding within the plankton. Upon hatching, the prolarvae drift as part of the ichthyoplankton community, where they begin exogenous feeding within a few days. The tiny size at emergence imposes high vulnerability to starvation and predation, and survival through this larval bottleneck is likely a key demographic filter. The pelagic larval duration typical of this genus spans several weeks, after which the postflexion larvae undergo metamorphosis and settle into benthic reef habitats as juvenile cardinalfish.

Direct observation of wild populations over multiple years has provided important demographic data on longevity. At the same water temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C] typical of its tropical habitat, the maximum longevity of Rhabdamia gracilis reaches approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years], a duration comparable to that recorded for other small apogonids. This suggests a relatively fast-paced life history for a fish of this body size. The low adult mortality associated with schooling behaviour and nocturnal sheltering among branching corals likely contributes to this extended survival. While the initial wet weight at birth is minuscule, the species grows rapidly through the juvenile stage, as indicated by the allometric relationship between standard length and body mass. The maximum adult size translates to an ultimate wet weight of 5.2 grams [Wwi = 5.2 grams], a value consistent with the length-weight scaling exponent derived from regional fisheries surveys.

Among these traits, the early onset of reproductive activity is notable: the wet weight at puberty of 0.56 grams [Wwp = 0.56 grams] represents only about 11 percent of the ultimate adult mass of 5.2 grams [Wwi = 5.2 grams], indicating that females begin spawning well before reaching final dimensions. This strategy buffers the population against unpredictable juvenile mortality by allowing multiple breeding opportunities over the 5-year lifespan (5 years) [am = 5 years] typical of the species at a temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C]. In field surveys, a standard length of 3.6 cm [Lp = 3.6 cm] serves as a practical threshold to distinguish immature from potentially reproductive individuals. The combination of early maturation and repeated clutch cycling throughout the warm season ensures stable recruitment even when per-event fecundity remains low, a pattern common among small, schooling coral-reef fishes.
